questions.q: In the case study, why does the admin reuse the existing 'BDR' profile for the six new reps instead of building a new one?
options: A known-good, already-tested profile is safer than improvising a new one, and six reps on a standard role doesn't justify building something new
Salesforce doesn't allow creating new profiles after an org is a year old
New profiles always require a support ticket to Salesforce
The BDR profile was the only one with a System Administrator license
questions.explain: The case study's reasoning is risk-based: reusing a profile that's already known to work is safer than building and testing a brand-new one for a routine hire.

questions.q: Why does the case study skip delegated administration for this scenario entirely?
options: Delegated administration can only be used for System Administrators
Six reps on one standard profile doesn't justify a separate delegated group — it's a tool suited to a different kind of scaling problem
Delegated administration requires a paid add-on this fictional org doesn't have
Delegated administration can't be combined with permission sets
questions.explain: The case study explicitly reasons that delegated administration doesn't fit this scenario's scale — it's a tool for handing off administrative work at a different scope than onboarding six reps onto an existing profile.

questions.q: Why does the admin filter the Dynamic Related List on Opportunities to open deals only, rather than leaving it unfiltered?
options: Unfiltered related lists are not supported in Lightning
To prevent reps from ever seeing closed Opportunities at all, under any view
Filtering is required by Salesforce for every related list on a custom record type
So a reused Account's old closed-lost Opportunities don't bury the team's live, active pipeline
questions.explain: This mirrors the Chapter 3 lesson on related list filters: an unfiltered list on a reused Account could bury the few open deals a rep needs under many old, irrelevant closed-lost records.

questions.q: Why does the admin build the profile, permission set, and record type changes in a sandbox first, even though the change 'feels routine'?
options: Sandboxes are required by law for any Salesforce configuration change
Production changes take longer to save than sandbox changes
Because the change touches a shared Account page layout that other teams already rely on, and a sandbox is where an unexpected side effect surfaces safely
Sandboxes automatically document every change for the admin
questions.explain: The case study explicitly notes the change touches a layout shared with other teams — exactly the kind of change where an unanticipated side effect could affect people well beyond the six new reps, which is why it's tested in a sandbox first.

questions.q: What does the admin check on day one after the new reps are live, and why?
options: Login History, to confirm all six reps successfully logged in — the fastest way to catch a licensing or access mistake before a rep has to ask for help
Field History Tracking, to see if any reports were deleted
Global Value Sets, to confirm picklist values are in sync
Email Templates, to confirm the welcome email was opened
questions.explain: Spot-checking Login History on day one is the case study's final step — it directly verifies that access and licensing were configured correctly, rather than waiting for a rep to report a problem.
